summary.text: 字 is traditionally analyzed as a child, 子, beneath a roof, 宀, with 子 also serving as a sound element. An early lexicographic account associates it with birth and nurture; today it commonly means “written character.” The history connecting those meanings remains unresolved.

formation.text: Phonosemantic in the traditional analysis: 宀 supplies the roof or indoor setting, while 子 depicts a child and is assigned a sound role. A bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀, though other analyses of the graph have been proposed.

components.text: Above 子, 宀 represents a roof or indoor setting in the traditional child-under-a-roof interpretation.
Below 宀, 子 depicts the child in the traditional interpretation and is also assigned a phonetic role.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin comparison does not establish the ancient sound relation. A reported Old Chinese comparison exists, but its exact dataset entries were not independently verified against the upstream dataset.

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 子 is zǐ and 字 is zì. A local reconstruction dataset reports 子 *[ts]əʔ / *tsəʔ and 字 *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s in its notation; these differ but have compatible consonant correspondences in that reconstruction.
sound.system: Old Chinese (Baxter–Sagart local dataset notation); Modern Mandarin

history.text: A bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀. A catalog records a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶, but this does not establish the inscription’s reading in context or make it the earliest attestation.

The traditional construction has been challenged, but the available account of that disagreement does not give enough detail to assess alternative readings. No graphic corruption or miscopying is identified.

uncertainties.text: The traditional child-under-a-roof analysis is attested as a historical explanation, but disagreement over the graph’s construction remains unresolved.

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: A Han lexicographic account gives birth or nurture as a meaning, but does not establish when that sense arose or whether the two glosses reflect one original lexical meaning.
字 commonly means a written character. The available material does not date the earliest use of this sense.
“Word” is also a recorded meaning; its chronology and relation to the birth or nurture sense are unresolved.

developments.text: A later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters; another account allows a distinct root or a derivation from producing or generating. The relationship and its chronology remain unresolved.

limitations.text: Dictionary glosses and the Han-era explanation that written forms multiply do not independently establish the chronology or development of the senses.

overview.text: 字 is traditionally explained as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀), with 子 also serving as a sound element. An early account associates it with birth and nurture; today it commonly means “written character.”

components.text: The roof element sets the indoor scene in the traditional interpretation.
The child appears in the scene; the traditional account also assigns 子 a sound role.

takeaway.text: The proposed link from birth and nurture to “written character” is an old explanation, but its development and chronology remain unresolved.

relationships.text: In the traditional construction, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting in the proposed child-under-a-roof scene.
In the traditional construction, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof.

The traditional account assigns 子 a sound role. Modern Mandarin 子 zǐ and 字 zì provide a current comparison; a local reconstruction dataset also reports compatible Old Chinese consonant correspondences, though its exact entries were not independently verified upstream.
